paper.title: UniIntervene: Agentic Intervention for Efficient Real-World Reinforcement Learning
paper.central_claim: A learned intervention module (future-conditioned action-value, temporal value-risk trigger, memory-guided goal-conditioned recovery) takes over most interventions in real-world human-in-the-loop RL, improving average success by 8.6% and cutting human interventions by 57% relative to HiL-SERL on five UR7e manipulation tasks.

provenance.notes: session_id/receipt_ref not obtainable inside this headless session. Blind boundary kept. Scope caveat for controller: no frontier LLM/VLM/coding-agent harness is present; the paper is a learned HiL-RL intervention module on a pi0.5-class policy. Record is scored as reviewed; controller/Opus may reclassify as out_of_scope under docs/EVIDENCE.md.

evidence.quote: we propose UniIntervene, an agentic intervention model that detects unproductive exploration and autonomously recovers the policy toward high-value states, taking over the bulk of interventions from human operators.
neither line addresses the dominant source of human cost in HiL-RL: rollouts that are not unsafe yet fail to progress, leaving human takeover as the only resort.
so the policy still spends substantial interactions in low-value states before a human is solicited
with \tau_{\mathrm{int}} a fixed threshold
evidence.support_explanation: execution rule: policy action unless intervention score exceeds a fixed threshold, then recovery action

evidence.quote: a proxy value function pre-trained offline on successful and failed trajectories
evidence.support_explanation: trigger and retrieval depend on an offline proxy value trained on success and failure trajectories

evidence.quote: We admit an entry only when the proxy value of the future state exceeds a threshold
supervised by behavior cloning on rollout segments connecting each
evidence.support_explanation: recovery policy trained by BC on segments from intervention state to later high-value state

evidence.quote: We evaluate UniIntervene on five real-world manipulation tasks with a UR7e robotic arm, where human interventions are provided via a SpaceMouse.
SR is measured over 20 evaluation episodes per task after training and reported as the percentage of successful episodes.
IR is computed over three independent training runs as the ratio between the total number of intervention steps and the total number of robot interaction steps.
evidence.support_explanation: IR definition; 3 runs; does not say whether autonomous interventions are excluded

evidence.quote: All baselines and UniIntervene are evaluated under the same robot platform, task initialization protocol, and SpaceMouse-based intervention interface.
evidence.support_explanation: control statement; no training-budget parity stated

evidence.quote: UniIntervene achieves the best success rate on every task and the lowest intervention rate overall, improving average success by 8.6% while cutting human interventions by 57% relative to HiL-SERL.
FA-RL reduces intervention by predicting failures, yet its trigger is tied to explicit failure signals
evidence.support_explanation: closest baseline and its stated limitation

evidence.support_explanation: "Intervention steps" is not said to exclude UniIntervene's own autonomous recoveries; whether IR and "human interventions" count the same events for all methods cannot be checked in the available text.

Average SR 88 vs 81 is +7 points, i.e. 8.6% relative; the abstract/caption phrase "improves ... by 8.6%" is a relative change, 57% fewer interventions is 14.6 vs 34.3. Arithmetic consistent; reading as points would be wrong.

How the proxy value, risk head, memory and recovery policy are trained and refreshed relative to the online RL loop (Table 2 has an "Online RL" column), what training budget the baselines get, and how many entries the memory holds are not specified in the available text (Appendix absent).

signatures.object: Intervention decision and recovery inside a real-world HiL-RL loop over a VLA-style policy (pi_theta)
signatures.information: Observation, instruction, current action; proxy value trained offline on success/failure trajectories; human operator remains available via SpaceMouse
signatures.operation: Predict latent next-state from (o,l,a) -> twin value head -> windowed value-shortfall risk -> intervention score; if score >= fixed threshold execute recovery chunk from goal-conditioned policy toward a memory-retrieved goal state
signatures.output: Recovery action chunk replacing the policy action
signatures.conditions: Rollout stagnates without being unsafe; similar past intervention episodes in memory
signatures.feedback: Value dynamics over a recent window
signatures.selection_rule: Trigger threshold on predicted risk; memory entry admitted only if proxy value of future state exceeds threshold; nearest memory key by cosine similarity
signatures.persistence: Recovery memory of (failure state, later high-value state) pairs from earlier rollouts; weights of value/risk/recovery heads
signatures.later_use: Retrieval at each trigger during online training and evaluation
signatures.claimed_effect: Average SR 88 vs 81 and IR 14.6 vs 34.3 versus HiL-SERL
signatures.failure_boundary: Poorly calibrated proxy value, uncovered failure modes, single embodiment, residual human supervision

signatures.information: Predicted future latent and a K-step sequence of value estimates
signatures.operation: R_t = (1 - V_t) * discounted sum of (epsilon - dV) over window; regress by risk head; score = sigmoid
signatures.conditions: Sustained low progress rate vs expected rate epsilon
signatures.claimed_effect: Removing TVR: F1 0.832, IR 16.9 on two tasks

gap.author_gap: HiL-RL remains intervention-intensive because rollouts that are unproductive but not unsafe leave human takeover as the only resort; prior work either reuses intervention data better or avoids unsafe states without reasoning about progress.
gap.checked_gap: Consistent with the paper's own baseline numbers (HiL-SERL IR 34.3%, FA-RL 24.6%). The two prior lines are characterised only in the introduction; not checked against their papers.

gap.residue: Time and human takeovers consumed by sustained stagnation; remaining human need for rare/unsafe failures.
gap.stakes: Labour cost and scalability of real-world RL.
gap.method_response: Value-trend trigger plus retrieved-goal recovery policy to absorb stagnation episodes.
gap.remaining_gap: Generality beyond one embodiment/tabletop, calibration of proxy value, uncovered failure modes, comparison breadth, cost accounting.

matches.operation_match: Gate flags learner states; a teacher-like source corrects there. Here the corrector is a learned goal-conditioned policy and the human only handles the residual; no frontier LLM/VLM teacher, no harness.

unassigned: No frontier-model harness, tool interface, or teacher-student distillation: the central contribution (learned stagnation monitor and memory-guided recovery for HiL-RL) is not covered by an embodied-harness card; K603/K202 are weak analogies only.

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: Own-value-trend gate selecting states at which a corrector acts <-> gate-flagged learner states receiving teacher actions.
pattern_mapping.necessary_conditions: A corrector better than the learner at flagged states.
pattern_mapping.differences: Corrector is learned and trained from past human-intervention segments; no frontier/black-box teacher; policy is not a harness-run model. Weak mapping, not forced into a card.

claims.text: UniIntervene improves average success by 8.6% and cuts human interventions by 57% relative to HiL-SERL.
claims.setting: UR7e, five tasks, SpaceMouse intervention, pi0.5 policy
claims.baseline_control: pi0.5 SFT (20 demos), HiL-SERL, HiL-SERL+FA-RL; method built on HiL-SERL
claims.selection_vs_test: Same tasks for training and evaluation; proxy value and memory built from their rollouts
claims.result_denominator: SR over 20 evaluation episodes per task; IR over three runs, steps ratio
claims.allowed_conclusion: On these five tasks the method has lower reported IR and higher reported SR than the compared baselines; 8.6% is relative (+7 points) from 20-episode estimates without intervals.

claims.text: The value-risk critic is the most critical module; future prediction and memory goal improve recovery quality.
claims.result_denominator: 20 episodes per task assumed; F1 and IR
claims.allowed_conclusion: Component removals lower reported SR/IR on two tasks; effect sizes are 1-3 episodes.

assessment.strongest_supported_claim: On five tabletop UR7e tasks, adding the module to HiL-SERL is reported to give higher final SR (88 vs 81 average) and lower intervention rate (14.6 vs 34.3), from 20 evaluation episodes per task.
assessment.not_claimed: Author-reported only; not reproduced; no transfer-level claim supported.

G.reason: Specific, checkable bottleneck: HiL-RL cost is dominated by non-progressing but not unsafe rollouts, with two nearest lines (intervention-data reuse; reset-free/recovery/safety-critic) and baselines HiL-SERL and FA-RL (E002,E003,E015). Baseline IR is measured (34.3%, up to 49.8%). Related work and references are absent, so lineage beyond intro/baselines cannot be bound to versions.

M.reason: Each component answers a stated sub-problem: future-conditioned value for sparse reward, windowed shortfall risk to separate stagnation from transient dips, retrieval of verified goal plus goal-conditioned control to resolve under-specified recovery. Ablation predictions are distinguishable (trigger trend vs instantaneous value; memory goal lowers SR with F1 unchanged) (E018,E019). Weak points: trigger validity rests on an offline proxy value that needs success and failure trajectories (E005,E020); "agentic" is not substantiated beyond a learned module.

X.reason: Main steps and the execution rule are described (E004,E005,E006,E007), but the integration with online RL (when each module is trained/refreshed, memory growth, how interventions of both kinds feed the policy update), thresholds/window values and training budget are not specified in the available text (E026); the recovery gate is validated qualitatively on two episodes (E016). Failure boundaries are acknowledged (E020,E021,E022).

E.measurement.reason: SR is over 20 real-robot episodes (E009) but the per-task success criterion and who judges it, the labels behind offline intervention F1, and baseline settings are deferred to appendices not in the fixed material; IR definition does not say whether autonomous recoveries are excluded (E024). Cannot resolve.

E.causality.reason: Same platform, initialization and intervention interface across methods (E011) and one-at-a-time removal of four components on two tasks (E017,E018). Gaps: ablation on 2 of 5 tasks with 20 episodes, so 95 vs 85 is two episodes; no stated training-budget/data parity (extra offline proxy-value data may be unavailable to baselines) (E026); FA-RL is stacked on HiL-SERL, not a matched alternative trigger.

E.holdout.reason: Claim is per-task training efficiency on five tasks; evaluation uses the training tasks with an initialization protocol, proxy value and memory are built from those tasks' rollouts, no held-out tasks/scenes/embodiments (E021). Scope of the claim is matched to this, but no dev/test or overlap description.

E.statistics.reason: Point estimates only: SR from 20 episodes per task, IR from three runs without spread, ablation single set of numbers; many differences are 1-2 episodes (E009,E010,E013,E014).

E.cost.reason: The claimed cost (human intervention rate) is measured against baselines (E013,E014), but compute, training time/steps, extra data for the proxy value, and whether IR counts autonomous interventions are not reported (E024,E026).
